p.src: Now Sun Wukong descended from the clouds and gave his master a full account of how the Bodhisattva had borrowed the boy and Laozi had taken back his treasures. Tripitaka thanked him over and over. Resolutely devoting himself to the pilgrimage and ready to risk his life on the journey west, he climbed into the saddle. Zhu Bajie shouldered the baggage, Friar Sand took hold of the horse's bridle, and Sun Wukong grasped his iron staff and cleared a path as they descended the lofty mountain and pressed onward. No words can fully recount how they slept beside rivers, ate in the wind, and journeyed through frost and dew.

p.src: After master and disciples had traveled for a long while, another mountain rose ahead to bar their way. From horseback Tripitaka called loudly, “Disciples, look how towering and rugged those mountains are. We must be especially vigilant, lest some demon calamity assail us again.” Wukong said, “Master, do not indulge in wild fears. Simply keep your nature settled and your spirit composed, and naturally nothing will happen.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, why is the road to the Western Heaven so very difficult? I remember that since leaving Chang'an, spring has ended and summer come, autumn has waned and winter arrived, through four or five years now. Why have we still not reached it?” Hearing this, Wukong laughed. “It is early yet, early yet! We have not even passed through the great gate.” Bajie said, “Brother, do not tell lies. Could there be such a gigantic gate in the human world?” Wukong said, “Brother, we are still wandering about inside the main hall.” Friar Sand laughed. “Elder Brother, do not frighten me with your boasting. Where could there be a hall so vast? Nowhere could one even buy a crossbeam big enough for it.” Wukong said, “Brothers, as old Sun sees it, take this blue sky for the roof tiles, the sun and moon for the window lattice, and the four ranges and five sacred peaks for beams and pillars; then heaven and earth are but one spacious hall.” On hearing this, Bajie said, “Enough, enough! Let us wander about a while and then go back.” Wukong said, “Stop talking nonsense and just follow old Sun along the road.”

p.src: The elder gazed ahead from horseback and saw, in a hollow among the mountains, tier upon tier of towers and rank upon rank of halls and pavilions. Tripitaka said, “Disciples, it is growing late. Fortunately, there are buildings not far away over there. They must belong to a hermitage, Daoist abbey, or Buddhist monastery. Let us all go there and ask for lodging tonight, then continue tomorrow.” Wukong said, “Master is right. Do not hurry. Let me first see whether the place is safe or dangerous.” The Great Sage leaped into the air and examined it closely. It was indeed the gate of a monastery. This is what he saw:

p.src: The elder gave his horse its head and rode straight forward until he reached the monastery gate. Wukong said, “Master, what monastery is this?” Tripitaka said, “My horse's hooves have only just stopped, and my toes are not even out of the stirrups, yet you ask me what monastery it is. How unreasonable!” Wukong said, “You have been a monk since childhood and must have studied the Confucian classics before you could expound the sutras. Only after becoming accomplished in letters and doctrine did you receive the Tang emperor's gracious favor. There are such enormous characters over the gate. How can you not recognize them?” The elder cursed him. “Impudent macaque! You speak without understanding. I was just urging my horse westward with the sunlight shining into my eyes. Besides, though there are characters over the gate, they are obscured by dust and grime, so I have not yet seen them.” Hearing this, Wukong bent at the waist and grew to a height of over twenty feet. He brushed away the dust with his hand and said, “Master, please look.” Above were five large characters reading: “Imperially Founded Baolin Monastery.” Wukong resumed his normal form and said, “Master, which of us should go into the monastery to ask for lodging?” Tripitaka said, “I shall go in. Your faces are ugly, your speech is coarse, and your natures are fierce and arrogant. If by chance you offend the monks here and they refuse us lodging, that would be most unfortunate.” Wukong said, “In that case, please go in, Master. There is no need to say more.”

p.src: On seeing them, Tripitaka nodded and sighed deeply. “If in my Eastern Land someone had also fashioned such great Bodhisattvas from clay and burned incense in worship before them, then I, your disciple, would never have gone to the Western Heaven.” While still sighing, he came within the second gate. There he saw images of the Four Great Heavenly Kings—Dhritarashtra, Vaishravana, Virudhaka, and Virupaksha—arrayed to signify favorable winds and timely rain in the east, north, west, and south. Beyond the second gate, he saw four tall pines, each crowned with a luxuriant canopy of green shaped like a parasol. Suddenly he raised his head and saw the Mahavira Hall. The elder joined his palms, took refuge in the Buddha, stretched himself out, and bowed. When he had finished bowing, he rose, passed around the Buddha platform, and came to the rear doorway. There he saw a rear-facing image of Guanyin delivering all beings from the Southern Sea. The walls were covered with figures skillfully modeled by master craftsmen: shrimps, fish, crabs, and turtles, poking out their heads and showing their tails as they frolicked amid the waves and tides of the sea. The elder nodded several more times and, heaving countless sighs, said, “What a pity! Even the scaled and armored creatures worship the Buddha; why, then, are human beings unwilling to cultivate the Way?”

p.src: While he was still praising what he saw, a temple attendant emerged from within the triple gate. The attendant suddenly noticed Tripitaka's extraordinary appearance and bearing, so unlike that of an ordinary man. He hurried forward, saluted him, and asked, “Master, where have you come from?” Tripitaka said, “This disciple was sent by the sovereign of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to worship the Buddha in the Western Heaven and seek the scriptures. We have now reached your honored region, and as night is approaching, I beg lodging for one night.” The attendant said, “Please do not take offense, Master, but I cannot decide the matter. I am merely the attendant here who sweeps the grounds, rings the bell, and performs the menial tasks. Inside is an elder master who manages the monastery. Wait while I go in and report your request to him. If he agrees to receive you, I shall come out and invite you in; if he does not, I would not dare keep you waiting.” Tripitaka said, “I am sorry to trouble you.”

p.src: The attendant hurried to the abbot’s quarters and reported, “Master, someone has come outside.” The monastic officer immediately rose, changed his clothes, straightened his Vairocana cap, put on his kasaya, and hurriedly opened the door to welcome the visitor. He asked the attendant, “Where has he come from?” The attendant pointed and said, “Is that not a man behind the main hall?” There stood Tripitaka, bareheaded, wearing a twenty-five-strip Dharma robe and a pair of mud-spattered monk’s shoes, leaning against the rear doorway. The monastic officer saw him and cried furiously, “You attendants deserve a beating! Do you not know that I am the monastic officer, and that I come out to welcome only gentlemen from the city who bring incense offerings? Why tell me, with more falsehood than truth, to come and receive a monk like this? Judging by his looks, he is no respectable man, but most likely a wandering monk who has come to beg lodging because night is falling. How could we allow him to disturb the abbot’s quarters? Tell him merely to squat beneath the front gallery. Why report him to me?” With that, he turned and went back inside.

p.src: When the elder heard this, tears filled his eyes and fell. “How pitiful, how pitiful! Truly, a man is despised once he leaves his native land. I entered the religious life as a child and became a monk. Never have I performed rites while eating meat and harboring wicked thoughts, nor read sutras in anger and corrupted my meditative heart; nor have I thrown tiles and bricks to damage a Buddha hall, or scraped true gold from an arhat’s face. Alas! How wretched I am! I know not in what former life I offended Heaven and Earth, that in this life I should constantly meet with wicked men. Monk, if you will not lodge us, so be it; but why speak such spiteful words and tell us to squat beneath the front gallery? It would be well if Pilgrim never heard of this; but if he did, that monkey would come in and give you such a thrashing with his iron staff that he would break both your shins.” The elder said, “Very well, very well. As the saying goes, ‘Courtesy and propriety come first among men.’ I shall go in and ask him, and see what he thinks.”

p.src: The master followed in the other’s footsteps and entered the gate of the abbot’s quarters. He saw that the monastic officer had taken off his ceremonial garments and sat there fuming. Whether he was reciting sutras or writing out a ritual service for someone was unclear, but papers and notes were piled upon his desk. The Tang Monk did not dare venture farther in, but stood in the courtyard, bowed, and called aloud, “Venerable abbot, this disciple offers his respects.” The monk was plainly displeased that he had come inside. He returned the greeting only halfheartedly and asked, “Where have you come from?” Tripitaka said, “This disciple was dispatched under imperial command from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, to worship the living Buddha in the Western Heaven and seek the scriptures. Passing through your honored region, we have been overtaken by night. We beg lodging for one night and shall depart tomorrow before the first light of dawn. I earnestly hope, venerable abbot, that you will accommodate us.” Only then did the monastic officer half rise and ask, “Are you that Tang Tripitaka?” Tripitaka replied, “I am unworthy of the name, but this disciple is he.” The monastic officer said, “If you are going to the Western Heaven for scriptures, how is it that you do not even know the road?” Tripitaka said, “This disciple has never before traveled the roads of your honored region.” He said, “Four or five li due west of here is a place called Thirty-Li Inn. There are households there that sell meals, and it is convenient and comfortable for lodging. It is inconvenient here, and we cannot properly accommodate monks who have come from afar.” Tripitaka joined his palms and said, “Abbot, the ancients said, ‘Hermitages, abbeys, and monasteries are the inns of us wandering monks; wherever there is a monastery gate, we are entitled to three sheng of rice.’ Why will you not let me stay? What manner of hospitality is this?” The monastic officer shouted angrily, “You wandering monks certainly know how to wag your glib tongues.” Tripitaka asked, “What do you mean by ‘glib tongues’?” The monastic officer said, “The ancients said, ‘When a tiger enters the city, every household shuts its door. Though it may bite no one now, it ruined its name in days gone by.’” Tripitaka asked, “How was that name ‘ruined in days gone by’?” He replied, “Some years ago, several groups of itinerant monks came and sat down at our monastery gate. Seeing how cold and destitute they were—each in torn clothes, some without shoes, all bareheaded and barefoot—I pitied their ragged condition and promptly invited them into the abbot’s quarters, gave them the seats of honor, treated them to a vegetarian meal, lent each of them an old garment, and allowed them to stay for several days. p.src: Hearing these words, Tripitaka thought to himself, “How wretched! Could this disciple of yours possibly be such a spineless monk?” He wanted to weep, but feared that the old monk of the monastery would laugh at him. So he merely tugged at his robe and secretly wiped away his tears, swallowed his anger in silence, and hurried outside to meet his three disciples. Seeing anger upon his master’s face, Pilgrim stepped forward and asked, “Master, did the monks in the temple beat you?” The Tang Monk replied, “They did not beat me.” Bajie said, “They certainly did; otherwise, why is there a sob in your voice?” Pilgrim asked, “Did they curse you?” The Tang Monk said, “They did not curse me either.” Pilgrim said, “If they neither beat nor cursed you, why are you so distressed? Surely you are not homesick?” The Tang Monk said, “Disciple, they cannot accommodate us here.” Pilgrim laughed. “Are they Daoists here, then?” The Tang Monk said angrily, “Daoists dwell in abbeys; only monks dwell in monasteries.” Pilgrim said, “You are no good at this. If they are monks, then they are of the same fellowship as us. As the saying goes, ‘All who gather beneath the Buddha are people joined by affinity.’ Sit here for a while and let me go inside to see.”

p.src: The fine Pilgrim pressed down the golden fillet upon his head, tightened the skirt about his waist, took up his iron staff, and went straight to the Great Hero Hall. Pointing at the three Buddha images, he said, “You may be false images molded from clay and gilded, but can there be no divine response within you? I, Old Sun, am escorting the holy monk of the Great Tang to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the true scriptures. Tonight we have come especially to lodge here, so make haste and announce our names for us. If they refuse to lodge us, I shall smash your golden bodies to pieces with a volley of blows and make you reveal your true forms of common clay.”

p.src: While the Great Sage was raging at the front and talking wild nonsense in his fierce stance, an attendant who was burning the evening incense came carrying several lighted sticks to place in the censer before the Buddha. Pilgrim barked at him, frightening him into a fall. He scrambled up, saw Pilgrim’s face, and fell over once more. Terrified, he stumbled and rolled all the way into the abbot’s quarters, where he reported, “Master, another monk has come outside.” The monastic officer said, “You pack of attendants all deserve a beating. I already told you to make them squat beneath the front gallery. Why report them again? Say another word and you will receive twenty strokes.” The attendant said, “Master, this monk is different from the other one. He looks vicious and violent, without a shred of decency.” The monastic officer asked, “What does he look like?” The attendant replied, “He has round eyes, protruding ears, a face covered in hair, and the beak of the Thunder God. He holds a staff in his hand and is gnashing his teeth fiercely, looking for someone to beat.” The monastic officer said, “Let me go out and see.”

The attendant replied, “He has round eyes, protruding ears, a face covered in hair, and the beak of the Thunder God.
He holds a staff in his hand and is gnashing his teeth fiercely, looking for someone to beat.”
The monastic officer said, “Let me go out and see.”

p.src: He opened the door, only for the Pilgrim to barge straight in. He truly was hideous: a lopsided, craggy face, two yellow eyes, a jutting brow, and tusks growing outward. He was like a crab, with his flesh inside and his bones outside. The old abbot was so alarmed that he shut the door of his quarters. The Pilgrim caught up and smashed the door panel with a thump, saying, “Hurry and clean a thousand tidy rooms for Old Sun to sleep in.” Hiding inside, the abbot said to the attendant, “No wonder he looks so ugly—his boasting must have twisted his face into that shape. Including the abbot’s quarters, the Buddha hall, the bell and drum towers, and both cloisters, this place has fewer than three hundred rooms altogether. Yet he wants a thousand rooms to sleep in—where could we possibly find them?” The attendant said, “Master, I have already been frightened out of my wits. Answer him however you see fit.” Trembling all over, the abbot called loudly, “Venerable traveler seeking lodging, our little temple on this desolate mountain is ill-equipped and dares not keep you. Please lodge elsewhere.”

p.src: The Pilgrim transformed his staff until it was as thick as a washbasin and planted it bolt upright in the courtyard. “Monk, if this place is inconvenient, then you move out.” The abbot said, “This is the temple where we have lived since childhood. Our grandmaster passed it to our master, and our master passed it to us; we in turn must hand it down to future generations. Who knows where that fellow comes from? He barges in recklessly and orders us to move out!” The attendant said, “My lord, this is a dreadful predicament. We had better move out—the cudgel has already forced its way through the door.” The abbot said, “Do not talk nonsense. There are four or five hundred monks here, young and old. Where could we move to? Even if we moved out, we would have nowhere to live.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim said, “Monk, if you have nowhere to move, send one man out so I can demonstrate my staff.” The old abbot called to the attendant, “Go out and let him demonstrate his staff on you.” The attendant panicked. “Mercy, master! You want me to be the target for a great pole like that?” The old abbot said, “‘Maintain an army for a thousand days to use it on one.’ Why will you not go out?” The attendant said, “Never mind being struck by that pole—even if it merely toppled over, it would crush me into pulp.” The old abbot said, “Never mind its crushing you. Standing there in the courtyard, if someone forgot about it while walking at night, one collision would knock a great hole in his head.” The attendant said, “Master, if you know how formidable it is, why send me out to serve as his demonstration?” Thus the two of them began wrangling inside.

p.src: Hearing them, the Pilgrim said, “That really will not do. If I kill one of them with a single blow, my master will blame me for committing violence again. Let me find something else to strike and show you.” He suddenly looked up and saw a stone lion outside the abbot’s door. Raising his staff, he brought it down with a resounding crash and smashed the lion to powder and rubble. The abbot saw it through a crack in the window. His bones went soft and his sinews numb with terror, and he hurriedly wriggled under the bed; the attendant crawled into the opening beneath the stove, crying without cease, “Mercy! That staff is heavy, far too heavy to withstand! Have mercy, have mercy!” The Pilgrim said, “Monk, I will not strike you. Let me ask you: how many monks are there in this temple?” Trembling all over, the abbot replied, “There are two hundred and eighty-five quarters in all, housing five hundred ordained monks with official certificates.” The Pilgrim said, “Go quickly and assemble all five hundred monks in perfect order. Have them put on their long robes and go out to welcome my master from the Tang court. Then I will not strike you.” The abbot said, “Mercy, master! If you will not strike us, we would carry him in on our shoulders if need be.” The Pilgrim said, “Go at once.” The abbot called to the attendant, “Never mind saying you were frightened out of your wits—even if your very heart has burst with fear, go and summon all the men to welcome our venerable lord, the Tang monk.”

p.src: The attendant had no choice. Risking his life, he dared not pass through the door but crawled out through a dog hole at the rear. He went straight to the main hall, beating the drum on the east side and striking the bell on the west. When bell and drum sounded together, the monks of every rank in both cloisters were startled and came to the hall, asking, “It is neither early morning nor evening. Why are you ringing the bell and beating the drum?” The attendant said, “Change your clothes quickly, form ranks behind the old master, and go beyond the monastery gate to welcome a great lord from the Tang realm.” The assembled monks duly formed neat ranks and went out through the gate to welcome him. Some had put on cassocks; some wore their short clerical robes; those without either wore straight robes shaped like great bells; and the very poorest, who had no long robes, joined two waistcloths together and draped them over their bodies. Seeing one of them, the Pilgrim asked, “Monk, what sort of garment are you wearing?” Frightened by his hideous appearance, the monk said, “Mercy, master! Do not strike me; let me explain. The cloth was obtained by begging in the city. There is no tailor here, so I made it myself into this ‘poor man’s wrap.’”

p.src: The Pilgrim chuckled inwardly on hearing this, then herded the monks outside the monastery gate and made them kneel. The abbot kowtowed and called loudly, “Venerable Lord Tang, please come and sit in the abbot’s quarters.” Seeing this, Bajie said, “Master, you are really no good at all. When you went in, your eyes were brimming with tears and your lower lip hung down far enough to hold an oil bottle. How did Elder Brother manage so cleverly to make them kowtow and come welcome us?” Tripitaka said, “You fool, you understand nothing of propriety. As the saying goes, ‘Even ghosts fear a wicked man.’” Seeing them kowtow in homage, the Tang monk felt deeply embarrassed. Stepping forward, he said, “Gentlemen, please rise.” The monks knocked their heads upon the ground and said, “My lord, if you will ask your disciple to show mercy and not wield that pole, we would gladly kneel for a month.” The Tang monk called, “Wukong, do not strike them.” The Pilgrim said, “I have not struck them. Had I done so, their roots would have been severed by now.” Only then did the monks rise. Some led the horse, some carried the luggage; they bore the Tang monk aloft, carried Bajie on their backs, and supported the Sand Monk. All together they entered the monastery gate, proceeded to the abbot’s quarters at the rear, and sat down according to rank.

p.src: The monks once more bowed in homage. Tripitaka said, “Abbot, please rise. There is no need for further ceremony; you shame this poor monk with such deference. You and I are both disciples of the Buddha.” The abbot said, “My lord is an imperial envoy from the superior kingdom, yet this humble monk failed to come out and welcome you. Now that you have reached this desolate mountain, my vulgar eyes failed to recognize your honored person when chance brought us together. May I ask, my lord: on your journey, do you eat vegetarian food, or do you eat meat? Then we may go prepare your meal.” Tripitaka said, “We eat vegetarian food.” The abbot said, “Disciple, this fierce-looking master surely enjoys meat.” The Pilgrim said, “We too eat vegetarian food. We have abstained from meat since our mothers’ wombs.” The monk exclaimed, “Mercy, master! Does such a fearsome brute eat vegetarian food too?” One rather bold monk stepped forward and asked, “Since the masters eat vegetarian food, how much rice must we cook to provide enough?” Bajie said, “You miserly monk, why even ask? Have every household cook one picul of rice.” All the monks panicked and hurried away to scrub the pots and stoves, while every quarter began preparing tea and food. They raised bright lamps high, set out tables and chairs, and entertained the Tang monk.

p.src: When master and disciples had finished their evening meal, the monks cleared away the utensils. Tripitaka thanked them, saying, “Venerable abbot, we have greatly imposed upon your honored monastery.” The monastic official replied, “Not at all, not at all. Our hospitality has been poor, very poor.” Tripitaka asked, “Where are my disciples and I to rest?” The monastic official said, “Your Reverence need not be anxious. This humble monk has already made arrangements.” He called out, “Attendant, how many men are over there awaiting orders?” The attendant replied, “Master, there are some.” The monastic official ordered, “Send two of them to prepare fodder and feed the Tang master’s horse. Send several others ahead to sweep those three meditation rooms clean, lay out the beds and curtains, and quickly invite Their Reverences to retire.”

p.src: The attendants obeyed, and when everything was in order, they came to invite the Tang master to retire. Master and disciples led the horse and shouldered the luggage, left the abbot’s quarters, and went straight to the meditation hall. Looking inside, they saw it brightly lit, with four rattan beds laid out at its two ends. Seeing this, Monkey called the attendant responsible for the fodder and had him bring it into the hall. He tethered the white horse there and told all the attendants to leave. Tripitaka sat in the middle. Under the lamplight, five hundred monks stood in two ranks, all waiting upon him and not daring to withdraw. Tripitaka rose slightly and said, “Gentlemen, please return to your quarters, so that this poor monk may retire at ease.” But the monks absolutely dared not leave. The monastic official stepped forward and instructed them, “Wait until His Reverence is settled for the night before returning.” Tripitaka said, “I am already settled. Please, all of you, return.” Only then did they dare to disperse.

p.src: Hearing this, Monkey stepped forward and replied, “Master, you know only the moonlight’s splendor and let your heart dwell upon your native home, but you do not understand the moon’s true meaning: it embodies the measures and principles of the prenatal Way. On the thirtieth day, the metal of its yang soul is wholly dispersed and the water of its yin essence fills the orb. Thus it is entirely black and without light, and is called the ‘dark moon.’ At that time it joins with the sun, and during the two days between the dark moon and the new moon, it receives the sun’s light and conceives. On the third day the first yang appears, and on the eighth the second yang is born. Then the soul is half present within the essence, and the moon is level as a taut cord; hence it is called the ‘first quarter.’ By the fifteenth day all three yangs are complete, so the moon is perfectly round; hence it is called the ‘full moon.’ On the sixteenth day the first yin is born, and on the twenty-second the second yin arises. Then the essence is half present within the soul, and the moon is level as a taut cord; hence it is called the ‘last quarter.’ By the thirtieth day all three yins are complete, and once again it is the ‘dark moon.’ This is the meaning of prenatal gathering and refinement. If we can nurture the two eights and bring the nine times nine to completion, then seeing the Buddha will be easy, and returning to our native field will be easy as well. A poem says:

p.src: Tripitaka said, “Very well. You disciples have had a hard journey, so go to sleep first. I shall stay and recite this scroll of scripture for a while.” Monkey said, “Master, you are mistaken. You entered religion in childhood and became a monk. Which of the scriptures you learned then do you not know by heart? Moreover, you received the Tang emperor’s decree to journey to the Western Heaven, see the Buddha, and obtain the true scriptures of the Great Vehicle. Now the task is not yet accomplished, you have not seen the Buddha, and you have not obtained the scriptures. What scripture can you be reciting?” Tripitaka replied, “Ever since I left Chang’an, I have trudged onward every morning and hurried along every day. I fear I may have grown rusty in the scriptures I learned as a child. Fortunately, I have leisure tonight, so let me review them.” Monkey said, “If that is what you mean, we shall go to sleep first.” The three of them each lay down upon a rattan bed. The elder closed the meditation-hall door, raised the silver lamp’s wick, opened his scripture, and silently read and recited. Indeed:
